newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi warns opposition against violence.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi warns opposition against violence.

text.p: Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi warned opposition politicians on Wednesday not to break the law in the run-up to elections after police broke up a banned opposition rally last weekend.
Reform and opposition groups under the National Convention Assembly (NCA) banner pulled back from an earlier declaration they would hold an "illegal" rally in the coastal city of Mombasa on Saturday.

The NCA, a coalition of opposition parties, human rights groups and church leaders, said it had yet to take a final decision on the Mombasa meeting, called to press for a minimum package of constitutional reforms before elections later this year.
Security forces last Saturday broke up an NCA rally declared illegal by the government, sparking two days of rioting in the capital that left one person dead and scores of shops and stalls looted.
"I warn opposition politicians they should not move around thinking Kenya is just a free-for-all," said Moi on his return from an Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe.
"From now henceforth law and order will be maintained by the government," he said.

At a state rally last Sunday in Nairobi's Uhuru Park, Moi said he would replace the Public Order Act that requires groups to obtain permits for meetings with a new bill, but did not specify its contents.
The NCA said in April it would no longer apply for licences for its rallies, setting the stage for renewed confrontation in Mombasa if the rally is held in breach of the law.

"The Mombasa rally has not been decided. This is a decision that can only be made by the National Convention Executive Council, which doesn't meet until tomorrow (Thursday)," joint NCA chairman Kivutha Kibwana told Reuters.
He added that an earlier announcement about the rally was simply a "suggestion" for the NCA to consider.

Moi's airport reception, attended by traditional choirs and dancers, a military marching band and most of the government, stood in marked contrast to Saturday's protests, broken up by police who fired teargas and fought running battles with demonstrators.
"My people tend to blame me for not talking to the opposition but how can I discuss with people who have got opposite opinions, who don't believe in peace?" Moi said.
Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, must call elections in 1997 pitting the ruling KANU party against an opposition fractured along ethnic and personal lines.
Diplomats said the proposed rally next Saturday and calls for constitutional change could serve to galvanise the opposition prior to the election.

"Events like Uhuru Park get the opposition leaders together when normally they are not on speaking terms. All the same old jealousies are lurking under the surface. But while there are battles to be fought they are on the same side," a western diplomat said.
The NCA wants review or repeal of six laws including the Public Order Act, reviled as an instrument of suppression. It is also demanding greater access to state-controlled media.
